# Design a Flight/Hotel Booking System

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `Expedia • Booking.com` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> You do not own the inventory. Every seat and every room is a live fact owned by an external airline or hotel system that you cannot query fast enough for every search, so the entire design is a bet on how ==stale a cached price== is allowed to be before you show a customer a lie.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a travel booking platform like Expedia: a user searches for flights
or hotels by route/dates, sees live prices and availability aggregated
from many different airlines and hotel chains, and can book a specific
option. Design the system end to end, including how it deals with the
fact that the actual inventory lives on someone else's servers.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Do we own and manage the inventory (our own hotels/flights), or are we aggregating live data from third-party supplier APIs?
*Why it matters:* This decides the whole architecture. Owning inventory means one strongly consistent database can be the source of truth. Aggregating from suppliers means every price and availability figure is, at best, a recent cache of a system we don't control and can't lock.

#### Q: When a user clicks 'book,' can we guarantee the price and seat they saw in search results is actually still available?
*Why it matters:* It usually can't be guaranteed, because the search result came from a cache. This forces a re-confirm step against the live supplier at booking time, and the design must handle the case where that re-confirm fails (price changed or sold out) gracefully rather than silently.

#### Q: How many suppliers do we integrate with, and do they all support real-time inventory queries, or do some only offer periodic batch feeds?
*Why it matters:* A supplier with a real-time API can be queried live for high-value confirms. A supplier that only pushes a nightly CSV feed forces us to trust a much staler cache for that inventory, which changes how confident the UI can be about availability.

#### Q: Is overbooking (selling a seat/room that turns out to be unavailable) something we must never do, or is a low, budgeted rate acceptable with compensation, the way airlines already operate?
*Why it matters:* Zero-overbooking requires synchronous confirmation with the supplier on every single booking, which is slow and can fail under supplier load. A budgeted overbooking tolerance allows more aggressive caching and a much faster, more available booking flow.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can search flights by origin, destination, and dates, or hotels by location and date range, and see a ranked list of live-ish prices and availability.
- A user can select a specific flight/room and complete a booking, paying and receiving a confirmation.
- A user can view and cancel their existing bookings.
- The system aggregates results from multiple third-party supplier APIs into one unified search response.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Search must return results in a couple of seconds even though it's fanning out to many external suppliers, some of which are slow or occasionally down.**
- **A confirmed booking must never be sold twice (no double-booking of the same seat/room), even under concurrent requests for the last remaining inventory.**
- **The system must degrade gracefully when an individual supplier is slow or unreachable, showing results from the suppliers that did respond rather than failing the whole search.**
- **Cached prices shown in search must be refreshed often enough that the rate of 'sorry, that price changed' at checkout stays low, since it is the single biggest driver of user distrust.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 20 million searches per day across flights and hotels combined
- Each search fans out to roughly 8 supplier APIs on average, with a per-supplier timeout of 1.5 seconds
- 1 in 400 searches converts to an actual booking (0.25% conversion), a realistic travel industry figure
- Peak traffic (holiday booking windows) runs at roughly 6x the daily average

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Average search QPS:** 20,000,000 / 86,400 seconds ≈ 230 searches/sec average
- **Peak search QPS:** 230 * 6 ≈ 1,400 searches/sec at peak, each fanning out to 8 suppliers ≈ 11,200 outbound supplier calls/sec at peak
- **Bookings per day:** 20,000,000 / 400 ≈ 50,000 bookings/day ≈ 0.6 bookings/sec average, tiny compared to search volume
- **Cache freshness budget:** If a cached fare is refreshed every 5 minutes and a route is searched 50 times in that window, one supplier call now serves 50 searches instead of 50, a 50x reduction in outbound supplier load at the cost of up to 5 minutes of staleness

*Capacity Takeaway:* Search traffic outnumbers booking traffic by roughly 400 to 1, and each search would naively require a live round trip to 8 external systems we don't control, so the entire architecture is built around a supplier-response cache with a short TTL that absorbs almost all search load, reserving the one live, synchronous supplier call for the moment a user actually tries to book.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
A search request hits the app tier, which checks the offers_cache first;
cache misses (or expired entries) trigger a fan-out to live supplier APIs
in parallel with a bounded timeout, and whichever suppliers respond in
time get merged, ranked, and returned, while background refresh workers
keep the cache warm for popular routes so most searches never wait on a
live supplier call at all. When a user actually books, the flow changes
character entirely: the app server makes one synchronous call to the
specific supplier to place a short-lived hold and re-confirm the real
price and availability, and only after that succeeds does it charge
payment and write a durable booking record, ensuring the thing we cached
for browsing is never the thing we trust for money.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Search (cached fan-out) and booking (live confirm) paths

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client"]:::client
    lb["Load Balancer"]:::server
    app["App Servers"]:::server
    cache["Offers Cache"]:::cache
    refresh["Cache Refresh Workers"]:::server
    supplier["Supplier APIs"]:::server
    bookingdb[("Bookings DB")]:::db
    queue>"Booking Events Queue"]:::queue
    client --> lb
    lb --> app
    app -->|"search: read"| cache
    refresh -.->|"poll popular routes"| supplier
    refresh -.->|"warm cache"| cache
    app -->|"book: live confirm"| supplier
    app -->|"write confirmed booking"| bookingdb
    app -.->|"notify/email"| queue
```

#### A booking request, step by step

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    classDef step fill:#1e293b,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#f8fafc;
    step_1["1. User clicks book on a cached offer (offer_id from search results)"]:::step
    step_2["2. App server places supplier hold (live, synchronous call)"]:::step
    step_1 --> step_2
    step_3["3. Supplier confirms hold or rejects (rejected -> show updated price/availability)"]:::step
    step_2 --> step_3
    step_4["4. Charge payment (only after hold succeeds)"]:::step
    step_3 --> step_4
    step_5["5. Write durable booking record (frozen offer snapshot)"]:::step
    step_4 --> step_5
    step_6["6. Release/confirm with supplier (finalize, send confirmation)"]:::step
    step_5 --> step_6
```

#### Outbound supplier calls vs cache TTL

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `GET` | `/api/search/flights` | Query params: origin, destination, depart_date, return_date?. Fans out to cached/live supplier data, returns a merged, ranked list of flight offers. |
| `GET` | `/api/search/hotels` | Query params: location, check_in, check_out, guests. Returns a merged, ranked list of hotel room offers. |
| `POST` | `/api/bookings` | Body: { offer_id, traveler_details, payment_token }. Re-confirms the offer live against the supplier, then books and charges payment, or returns a clear conflict if the offer is no longer available. |
| `GET` | `/api/bookings/{bookingId}` | Returns the confirmed booking details, confirmation number, and current status. |
| `POST` | `/api/bookings/{bookingId}/cancel` | Cancels the booking, triggers the supplier's cancellation flow and any applicable refund. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `offers_cache`
- `offer_id (generated, unique per cached result)`
- `supplier_id`
- `route_or_property_key (e.g. origin-dest-date, or hotel_id-checkin-checkout)`
- `price`
- `availability_count`
- `cached_at (timestamp, drives TTL expiry)`
*Notes:* A short-lived, disposable cache, never the source of truth. Rebuilt continuously by background refresh jobs polling supplier APIs for high-traffic routes/properties.

### Entity: `bookings`
- `booking_id (unique)`
- `user_id`
- `supplier_id`
- `supplier_confirmation_ref`
- `offer_snapshot (price and details at time of booking, frozen)`
- `status (pending, confirmed, cancelled, failed)`
- `created_at`
*Notes:* The durable source of truth for what a user actually bought, independent of whatever the cache said at search time.

### Entity: `supplier_inventory_lock`
- `supplier_id`
- `resource_key (seat or room identifier)`
- `held_by_booking_id`
- `expires_at`
*Notes:* A short-lived hold (a few minutes) taken on a specific supplier resource during the checkout flow, so two users confirming the same last seat don't both succeed.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Cached search results vs live supplier queries: what to trust when
Querying all 8 suppliers live on every search would be accurate but far too slow and would hammer supplier rate limits under real traffic. Caching aggressively makes search fast and cheap, but every cached price is a small lie about the present moment. The resolution is to split the two use cases: search is allowed to be wrong for a few minutes because it is just browsing, but the moment a user tries to spend money, the system pays the cost of one live, synchronous supplier round trip to re-verify before committing.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Always-live search: perfectly accurate prices, but supplier fan-out latency (often 1-2 seconds per supplier) makes search feel slow, and supplier rate limits get exhausted fast under real traffic
- Always-cached search: fast and cheap, but stale prices lead to a bad checkout experience where the price or availability quietly changed
- The hybrid used in production: cache for search (short TTL, background refresh for hot routes), live re-confirm only at the moment of booking, which is the one place staleness actually costs money

### Preventing the same seat or room from being sold to two people at once
Because the actual inventory lives on the supplier's system, we cannot simply put a row-level lock in our own database, the supplier's own concurrency control is the real source of truth. The practical approach is a **two-phase booking**: place a short-lived hold on the specific supplier resource (many airline/hotel APIs support exactly this), which reserves it for a few minutes, then confirm and charge payment before that hold expires, releasing the hold automatically if the user abandons checkout.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Optimistic booking (charge first, confirm with supplier after): faster checkout experience, but risks charging a customer for something that turns out to be sold out, requiring an awkward refund and apology
- Hold-then-confirm (reserve with supplier, then charge): slightly slower checkout (one extra round trip), but never charges for something unavailable, at the cost of depending on the supplier actually supporting a hold/reservation API, which not all of them do
- For suppliers with no hold API at all, the only honest option is to confirm and charge in the same synchronous call, accepting a small, budgeted rate of post-booking failures that get resolved by rebooking or refund, similar to how airlines already handle real-world overbooking

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- A single slow or down supplier can drag down every search that includes it; each supplier call needs an independent timeout and circuit breaker so one bad supplier degrades gracefully instead of stalling the whole fan-out.
- The background cache-refresh jobs for popular routes can themselves overwhelm a supplier's rate limits if not throttled per-supplier, so refresh scheduling needs its own per-supplier rate budget.
- Booking writes are low volume but must be strongly durable and idempotent, since retried booking requests (from a flaky client connection) must never create two charges or two bookings for the same attempt.
- As supplier count grows into the dozens or hundreds (common for hotel aggregation), the fan-out and ranking logic itself becomes a scaling concern; sharding suppliers across parallel worker pools keeps one large batch of suppliers from serializing behind another.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Treating the search cache as if it were authoritative== and skipping the live re-confirm step at booking time, leading to charging customers for inventory that's already gone.
- ⚠️ Querying all suppliers live and synchronously on every search, which looks correct in a demo but collapses under real traffic and real supplier rate limits.
- ⚠️ Designing the double-booking prevention entirely inside your own database, forgetting that the actual seat or room is a fact that lives on someone else's server.
- ⚠️ Not planning for partial supplier failure, so one slow airline API times out the entire search request instead of just being omitted from that response.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why can't you just put a row lock on the seat/room in your own database to prevent double-booking?**

> **Model Answer:** Because your database doesn't own the inventory, the supplier's system does. A lock in your database only prevents two of your own requests from racing each other, it does nothing to stop the supplier from independently selling that same seat through their own website or another travel platform at the same moment. The only real prevention is a hold placed directly against the supplier's system.

**Q: How would you decide the TTL for a cached fare?**

> **Model Answer:** By balancing supplier call volume against user-visible staleness: a shorter TTL means fresher prices but more outbound supplier calls (and more risk of hitting rate limits), a longer TTL means cheaper caching but more 'price changed at checkout' surprises. In practice this is tuned per route based on volatility, a high-demand holiday route might refresh every minute while a low-traffic route refreshes every 15.

**Q: What should happen when a user's booking fails at the live-confirm step because the price went up since they searched?**

> **Model Answer:** The booking should fail cleanly with a clear message showing the new price and asking the user to confirm again, rather than silently charging the new price or silently charging the old one. Never charge a price the supplier didn't actually confirm.

pages.content:
# Design a Flight/Hotel Booking System

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `Expedia • Booking.com` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> You do not own the inventory. Every seat and every room is a live fact owned by an external airline or hotel system that you cannot query fast enough for every search, so the entire design is a bet on how ==stale a cached price== is allowed to be before you show a customer a lie.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a travel booking platform like Expedia: a user searches for flights
or hotels by route/dates, sees live prices and availability aggregated
from many different airlines and hotel chains, and can book a specific
option. Design the system end to end, including how it deals with the
fact that the actual inventory lives on someone else's servers.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Do we own and manage the inventory (our own hotels/flights), or are we aggregating live data from third-party supplier APIs?
*Why it matters:* This decides the whole architecture. Owning inventory means one strongly consistent database can be the source of truth. Aggregating from suppliers means every price and availability figure is, at best, a recent cache of a system we don't control and can't lock.

#### Q: When a user clicks 'book,' can we guarantee the price and seat they saw in search results is actually still available?
*Why it matters:* It usually can't be guaranteed, because the search result came from a cache. This forces a re-confirm step against the live supplier at booking time, and the design must handle the case where that re-confirm fails (price changed or sold out) gracefully rather than silently.

#### Q: How many suppliers do we integrate with, and do they all support real-time inventory queries, or do some only offer periodic batch feeds?
*Why it matters:* A supplier with a real-time API can be queried live for high-value confirms. A supplier that only pushes a nightly CSV feed forces us to trust a much staler cache for that inventory, which changes how confident the UI can be about availability.

#### Q: Is overbooking (selling a seat/room that turns out to be unavailable) something we must never do, or is a low, budgeted rate acceptable with compensation, the way airlines already operate?
*Why it matters:* Zero-overbooking requires synchronous confirmation with the supplier on every single booking, which is slow and can fail under supplier load. A budgeted overbooking tolerance allows more aggressive caching and a much faster, more available booking flow.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can search flights by origin, destination, and dates, or hotels by location and date range, and see a ranked list of live-ish prices and availability.
- A user can select a specific flight/room and complete a booking, paying and receiving a confirmation.
- A user can view and cancel their existing bookings.
- The system aggregates results from multiple third-party supplier APIs into one unified search response.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Search must return results in a couple of seconds even though it's fanning out to many external suppliers, some of which are slow or occasionally down.**
- **A confirmed booking must never be sold twice (no double-booking of the same seat/room), even under concurrent requests for the last remaining inventory.**
- **The system must degrade gracefully when an individual supplier is slow or unreachable, showing results from the suppliers that did respond rather than failing the whole search.**
- **Cached prices shown in search must be refreshed often enough that the rate of 'sorry, that price changed' at checkout stays low, since it is the single biggest driver of user distrust.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 20 million searches per day across flights and hotels combined
- Each search fans out to roughly 8 supplier APIs on average, with a per-supplier timeout of 1.5 seconds
- 1 in 400 searches converts to an actual booking (0.25% conversion), a realistic travel industry figure
- Peak traffic (holiday booking windows) runs at roughly 6x the daily average

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Average search QPS:** 20,000,000 / 86,400 seconds ≈ 230 searches/sec average
- **Peak search QPS:** 230 * 6 ≈ 1,400 searches/sec at peak, each fanning out to 8 suppliers ≈ 11,200 outbound supplier calls/sec at peak
- **Bookings per day:** 20,000,000 / 400 ≈ 50,000 bookings/day ≈ 0.6 bookings/sec average, tiny compared to search volume
- **Cache freshness budget:** If a cached fare is refreshed every 5 minutes and a route is searched 50 times in that window, one supplier call now serves 50 searches instead of 50, a 50x reduction in outbound supplier load at the cost of up to 5 minutes of staleness

*Capacity Takeaway:* Search traffic outnumbers booking traffic by roughly 400 to 1, and each search would naively require a live round trip to 8 external systems we don't control, so the entire architecture is built around a supplier-response cache with a short TTL that absorbs almost all search load, reserving the one live, synchronous supplier call for the moment a user actually tries to book.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
A search request hits the app tier, which checks the offers_cache first;
cache misses (or expired entries) trigger a fan-out to live supplier APIs
in parallel with a bounded timeout, and whichever suppliers respond in
time get merged, ranked, and returned, while background refresh workers
keep the cache warm for popular routes so most searches never wait on a
live supplier call at all. When a user actually books, the flow changes
character entirely: the app server makes one synchronous call to the
specific supplier to place a short-lived hold and re-confirm the real
price and availability, and only after that succeeds does it charge
payment and write a durable booking record, ensuring the thing we cached
for browsing is never the thing we trust for money.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Search (cached fan-out) and booking (live confirm) paths

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client"]:::client
    lb["Load Balancer"]:::server
    app["App Servers"]:::server
    cache["Offers Cache"]:::cache
    refresh["Cache Refresh Workers"]:::server
    supplier["Supplier APIs"]:::server
    bookingdb[("Bookings DB")]:::db
    queue>"Booking Events Queue"]:::queue
    client --> lb
    lb --> app
    app -->|"search: read"| cache
    refresh -.->|"poll popular routes"| supplier
    refresh -.->|"warm cache"| cache
    app -->|"book: live confirm"| supplier
    app -->|"write confirmed booking"| bookingdb
    app -.->|"notify/email"| queue
```

#### A booking request, step by step

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    classDef step fill:#1e293b,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#f8fafc;
    step_1["1. User clicks book on a cached offer (offer_id from search results)"]:::step
    step_2["2. App server places supplier hold (live, synchronous call)"]:::step
    step_1 --> step_2
    step_3["3. Supplier confirms hold or rejects (rejected -> show updated price/availability)"]:::step
    step_2 --> step_3
    step_4["4. Charge payment (only after hold succeeds)"]:::step
    step_3 --> step_4
    step_5["5. Write durable booking record (frozen offer snapshot)"]:::step
    step_4 --> step_5
    step_6["6. Release/confirm with supplier (finalize, send confirmation)"]:::step
    step_5 --> step_6
```

#### Outbound supplier calls vs cache TTL

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `GET` | `/api/search/flights` | Query params: origin, destination, depart_date, return_date?. Fans out to cached/live supplier data, returns a merged, ranked list of flight offers. |
| `GET` | `/api/search/hotels` | Query params: location, check_in, check_out, guests. Returns a merged, ranked list of hotel room offers. |
| `POST` | `/api/bookings` | Body: { offer_id, traveler_details, payment_token }. Re-confirms the offer live against the supplier, then books and charges payment, or returns a clear conflict if the offer is no longer available. |
| `GET` | `/api/bookings/{bookingId}` | Returns the confirmed booking details, confirmation number, and current status. |
| `POST` | `/api/bookings/{bookingId}/cancel` | Cancels the booking, triggers the supplier's cancellation flow and any applicable refund. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `offers_cache`
- `offer_id (generated, unique per cached result)`
- `supplier_id`
- `route_or_property_key (e.g. origin-dest-date, or hotel_id-checkin-checkout)`
- `price`
- `availability_count`
- `cached_at (timestamp, drives TTL expiry)`
*Notes:* A short-lived, disposable cache, never the source of truth. Rebuilt continuously by background refresh jobs polling supplier APIs for high-traffic routes/properties.

### Entity: `bookings`
- `booking_id (unique)`
- `user_id`
- `supplier_id`
- `supplier_confirmation_ref`
- `offer_snapshot (price and details at time of booking, frozen)`
- `status (pending, confirmed, cancelled, failed)`
- `created_at`
*Notes:* The durable source of truth for what a user actually bought, independent of whatever the cache said at search time.

### Entity: `supplier_inventory_lock`
- `supplier_id`
- `resource_key (seat or room identifier)`
- `held_by_booking_id`
- `expires_at`
*Notes:* A short-lived hold (a few minutes) taken on a specific supplier resource during the checkout flow, so two users confirming the same last seat don't both succeed.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Cached search results vs live supplier queries: what to trust when
Querying all 8 suppliers live on every search would be accurate but far too slow and would hammer supplier rate limits under real traffic. Caching aggressively makes search fast and cheap, but every cached price is a small lie about the present moment. The resolution is to split the two use cases: search is allowed to be wrong for a few minutes because it is just browsing, but the moment a user tries to spend money, the system pays the cost of one live, synchronous supplier round trip to re-verify before committing.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Always-live search: perfectly accurate prices, but supplier fan-out latency (often 1-2 seconds per supplier) makes search feel slow, and supplier rate limits get exhausted fast under real traffic
- Always-cached search: fast and cheap, but stale prices lead to a bad checkout experience where the price or availability quietly changed
- The hybrid used in production: cache for search (short TTL, background refresh for hot routes), live re-confirm only at the moment of booking, which is the one place staleness actually costs money

### Preventing the same seat or room from being sold to two people at once
Because the actual inventory lives on the supplier's system, we cannot simply put a row-level lock in our own database, the supplier's own concurrency control is the real source of truth. The practical approach is a **two-phase booking**: place a short-lived hold on the specific supplier resource (many airline/hotel APIs support exactly this), which reserves it for a few minutes, then confirm and charge payment before that hold expires, releasing the hold automatically if the user abandons checkout.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Optimistic booking (charge first, confirm with supplier after): faster checkout experience, but risks charging a customer for something that turns out to be sold out, requiring an awkward refund and apology
- Hold-then-confirm (reserve with supplier, then charge): slightly slower checkout (one extra round trip), but never charges for something unavailable, at the cost of depending on the supplier actually supporting a hold/reservation API, which not all of them do
- For suppliers with no hold API at all, the only honest option is to confirm and charge in the same synchronous call, accepting a small, budgeted rate of post-booking failures that get resolved by rebooking or refund, similar to how airlines already handle real-world overbooking

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- A single slow or down supplier can drag down every search that includes it; each supplier call needs an independent timeout and circuit breaker so one bad supplier degrades gracefully instead of stalling the whole fan-out.
- The background cache-refresh jobs for popular routes can themselves overwhelm a supplier's rate limits if not throttled per-supplier, so refresh scheduling needs its own per-supplier rate budget.
- Booking writes are low volume but must be strongly durable and idempotent, since retried booking requests (from a flaky client connection) must never create two charges or two bookings for the same attempt.
- As supplier count grows into the dozens or hundreds (common for hotel aggregation), the fan-out and ranking logic itself becomes a scaling concern; sharding suppliers across parallel worker pools keeps one large batch of suppliers from serializing behind another.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Treating the search cache as if it were authoritative== and skipping the live re-confirm step at booking time, leading to charging customers for inventory that's already gone.
- ⚠️ Querying all suppliers live and synchronously on every search, which looks correct in a demo but collapses under real traffic and real supplier rate limits.
- ⚠️ Designing the double-booking prevention entirely inside your own database, forgetting that the actual seat or room is a fact that lives on someone else's server.
- ⚠️ Not planning for partial supplier failure, so one slow airline API times out the entire search request instead of just being omitted from that response.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups

> **Model Answer:** Because your database doesn't own the inventory, the supplier's system does. A lock in your database only prevents two of your own requests from racing each other, it does nothing to stop the supplier from independently selling that same seat through their own website or another travel platform at the same moment. The only real prevention is a hold placed directly against the supplier's system.

**Q: How would you decide the TTL for a cached fare?**

> **Model Answer:** By balancing supplier call volume against user-visible staleness: a shorter TTL means fresher prices but more outbound supplier calls (and more risk of hitting rate limits), a longer TTL means cheaper caching but more 'price changed at checkout' surprises. In practice this is tuned per route based on volatility, a high-demand holiday route might refresh every minute while a low-traffic route refreshes every 15.

**Q: What should happen when a user's booking fails at the live-confirm step because the price went up since they searched?**

> **Model Answer:** The booking should fail cleanly with a clear message showing the new price and asking the user to confirm again, rather than silently charging the new price or silently charging the old one. Never charge a price the supplier didn't actually confirm.

lesson.content:
# Design an Auction System (eBay)

> **Difficulty:** `MEDIUM` | **Target Companies:** `eBay` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> A bid is not just a write, it's a comparison-and-write against a value that a hundred other people might be racing to change at the exact same instant, so the entire design is about making 'is this the new highest bid' atomic under real concurrency, not about storing bids.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design an online auction system like eBay: a seller lists an item with a
starting price and an end time, buyers place bids, the highest bid at the
close of the auction wins. Support both manual bids and "auto-bid" (a
buyer sets a max they're willing to pay and the system bids incrementally
on their behalf up to that max). Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: How does auto-bidding (proxy bidding) actually work, does the system bid the minimum increment needed to stay ahead, up to the user's max?
*Why it matters:* This changes bid placement from a simple insert into a small state machine: every new manual bid can trigger an automatic counter-bid from an existing auto-bidder, which itself might trigger another, so the design needs to handle a bidding cascade within a single request, not just one write.

#### Q: What happens if two bids arrive at nearly the same instant, does strict ordering matter, and how do we prevent both from being accepted as 'the new highest'?
*Why it matters:* This is the core concurrency problem of the whole system. Without an atomic compare-and-set on the current highest bid, two concurrent requests can both read the same 'old highest' and both think they won, corrupting the auction state.

#### Q: Does the auction end time extend if a bid comes in during the last moments (anti-sniping), or is it a hard cutoff?
*Why it matters:* A hard cutoff makes 'close the auction' a simple scheduled job. Anti-sniping extension means closing an auction is itself a dynamic, bid-dependent decision, and the scheduling system has to be able to push its own deadline back in response to new writes.

#### Q: How many concurrent bidders does a single hot auction realistically see, is this closer to a handful of bidders or thousands racing on a single popular item?
*Why it matters:* A handful of bidders can be safely serialized with an ordinary database transaction. Thousands of concurrent bidders on one item turn that same row into a hot lock contention point, which changes the concurrency strategy from 'a transaction' to something that needs a queue or a dedicated serialization point per auction.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A seller can create an auction listing with a starting price, item details, and an end time.
- A buyer can place a manual bid on an active auction, which must exceed the current highest bid by at least the minimum increment.
- A buyer can set a maximum auto-bid amount, and the system automatically places incremental bids on their behalf to keep them winning, up to that maximum.
- The system determines and announces the winning bidder when an auction closes, and notifies outbid users promptly during the auction.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Bid placement must be strongly consistent: under concurrent bids for the same auction, exactly one bid is ever recorded as the current highest, no lost updates.**
- **Outbid notifications should reach affected users within a couple of seconds, close to real-time, since a delayed notification directly costs a bidder the auction.**
- **The system must remain available and responsive during the closing seconds of popular auctions, which is exactly when bid volume spikes hardest.**
- **Auction close timing must be reliable and precise, an auction that closes late or early is a direct, disputable integrity failure of the product.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 5 million active auctions at any time, average auction runs for 5 days
- Average auction receives 15 bids over its lifetime, but the top 1% of 'hot' auctions receive over 500 bids, concentrated heavily in the final minute
- 50 million bids placed per day platform-wide
- A hot auction in its final minute can see up to 20 bids/sec from a bidding war combined with auto-bid cascades

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Average bid write rate:** 50,000,000 / 86,400 seconds ≈ 580 bids/sec average across the whole platform, spread over millions of auctions so contention per auction is normally low
- **Peak contention on one hot auction:** 20 bids/sec sustained for the last 60 seconds of a hot auction means up to 1,200 competing writes against the same 'current highest bid' value in a single minute
- **Auto-bid cascade multiplier:** If 3 auto-bidders are active on one item, a single manual bid can trigger up to 2 additional automatic counter-bids in the same instant, roughly tripling the effective write rate on that one auction's hot path during a bidding war
- **Notification fan-out:** Each of the ~1,200 bids on a hot auction in its final minute potentially outbids the previous highest bidder, meaning up to 1,200 outbid notifications need to go out for that single item in that single minute

*Capacity Takeaway:* The platform-wide bid rate is modest, under 600 bids/sec on average, but the real problem is concentrated: a single hot auction's last 60 seconds can generate more write contention on one row than the rest of the platform generates in total, which is why per-auction bid serialization, not overall throughput, is the number that drives this architecture.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
A bid submitted to POST /bids does not go straight to a naive insert.
Instead, each auction has a single logical serialization point (either a
database row with optimistic concurrency control via the version field, or
a per-auction in-memory actor/queue for very hot auctions) that every bid
for that auction must pass through one at a time. The app server reads the
current highest bid and version, validates the new bid against it, and
attempts an atomic compare-and-set write; if it fails because another bid
won the race, it retries against the new current state. After a bid is
accepted, the system checks active auto-bid settings for that auction and
synchronously generates any necessary counter-bids through the same
serialization point, then publishes an outbid event asynchronously so the
previous highest bidder is notified without blocking the bid response
itself.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Bid placement through a per-auction serialization point

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client"]:::client
    lb["Load Balancer"]:::server
    app["App Servers"]:::server
    seq["Auction Bid Sequencer"]:::server
    auctiondb[("Auctions DB")]:::db
    bidsdb[("Bids History")]:::db
    queue>"Outbid Events Queue"]:::queue
    notify["Notification Workers"]:::server
    client --> lb
    lb --> app
    app -->|"submit bid"| seq
    seq -->|"CAS on current highest"| auctiondb
    seq -->|"append bid"| bidsdb
    seq -.->|"outbid event"| queue
    queue -.-> notify
```

#### A bid that triggers an auto-bid counter-bid

#### Choosing how to serialize bids on one auction

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  a["Expected concurrent bidders?"] --> b["Handful"]
  a --> c["Hundreds, hot auction"]
  b --> d["Ordinary DB transaction"]
  c --> e["Version-based compare-and-set"]
  e --> f["Conflicts under extreme load?"]
  f -->|"Yes"| g["Per-auction sequencer actor"]
  f -->|"No"| e
```

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/api/auctions` | Body: { item_details, starting_price, end_time }. Creates a new auction listing from the authenticated seller. |
| `POST` | `/api/auctions/{auctionId}/bids` | Body: { amount } for a manual bid, or { max_auto_bid } to set/update proxy bidding. Atomically validates against the current highest bid and either accepts or rejects with the current price. |
| `GET` | `/api/auctions/{auctionId}` | Returns the auction's current state: current highest bid (amount only, not the bidder's max), time remaining, and bid history. |
| `POST` | `/api/auctions/{auctionId}/watch` | Subscribes the authenticated user to real-time updates (outbid notifications, closing alerts) for this auction. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `auctions`
- `auction_id (unique)`
- `seller_id`
- `starting_price`
- `current_highest_bid_amount`
- `current_highest_bidder_id`
- `end_time (mutable if anti-sniping extension applies)`
- `status (active, closed, cancelled)`
- `version (optimistic concurrency token, incremented on every bid)`
*Notes:* The version field is what makes bid placement safe: a bid write includes a compare-and-set against the version it read, so two concurrent bids can never both succeed against the same stale state.

### Entity: `bids`
- `bid_id`
- `auction_id (indexed)`
- `bidder_id`
- `amount`
- `is_auto_bid (bool)`
- `placed_at (timestamp)`
*Notes:* An append-only history, never updated, so the full bid trail is always auditable, which matters a lot for dispute resolution.

### Entity: `auto_bid_settings`
- `auction_id`
- `bidder_id`
- `max_amount`
- `active (bool)`
*Notes:* Stores the private max a user is willing to pay. Never exposed to other bidders or the seller, only used internally to generate counter-bids.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Making 'place a bid' atomic under real concurrency
The naive approach, read the current highest bid, check the new bid beats it, then write, has a race condition: two concurrent requests can both read the same old highest bid, both pass validation, and both write, with the second write silently overwriting the first's win instead of being rejected. The fix is to never let 'check' and 'write' be two separate steps against data that can change between them.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Optimistic concurrency (compare-and-set on a version number): cheap most of the time since there's no lock held, but under very high contention (a hot auction's last seconds) many bids fail the compare-and-set and must retry, adding latency exactly when it matters most
- Pessimistic locking (a database row lock held for the duration of the check-and-write): guarantees correctness with no retries needed, but serializes every bid on a hot auction behind a lock, which becomes a throughput ceiling during exactly the bidding-war moments the system needs to handle best
- A dedicated per-auction sequencer (a single in-memory actor or partition that owns all bid processing for one auction_id): removes database lock contention entirely for that auction and processes bids strictly in arrival order, at the cost of needing that actor to be highly available itself, since if it fails, its auction's bidding stalls

### Auto-bid (proxy bidding) as a state machine, not a one-time action
A user sets a private maximum once, but the system must keep re-evaluating it every time someone else bids, automatically raising this user's effective bid by the minimum increment whenever they're outbid, up to their max, without the user doing anything. This means a single incoming manual bid can trigger a cascade: bid arrives, beats current highest, triggers auto-bidder A's counter-bid, which might beat auto-bidder B's max entirely (B loses, no further action) or trigger B's own counter-bid in turn.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Resolving the cascade synchronously within the same request that placed the triggering bid: the auction state is always fully consistent by the time any request returns, but a single bid can now take noticeably longer if it triggers several rounds of auto-bid cascades
- Resolving the cascade asynchronously via a queue: the original bid returns fast, but there's a brief window where the auction's displayed 'current highest' is stale relative to what it's about to become, which can confuse a user watching the auction in real time
- In practice, cascades are almost always shallow (2-3 rounds at most, since auto-bid maxes rarely tie exactly), so resolving synchronously through the same per-auction serialization point used for manual bids is usually both correct and fast enough

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- A single viral 'hot' auction is the worst case for this whole system, not average load; the per-auction serialization point (lock, version-CAS, or actor) needs to be evaluated for how it behaves at hundreds of bids per second on one auction_id, not how the platform behaves on average.
- Outbid notifications need to be pushed via websockets or long-polling for genuinely real-time delivery; a polling-based client checking every few seconds is not fast enough for a bidder to react before an auction closes.
- Anti-sniping extension logic (pushing end_time back when a bid lands in the closing seconds) must itself go through the same atomic update as the bid, otherwise two near-simultaneous late bids can race to extend the same auction inconsistently.
- The auction-closing job (scanning for auctions past end_time) needs to be exactly-once and crash-safe; a duplicate close can incorrectly notify a winner twice or double-charge, and a missed close can leave an auction silently open past its real deadline.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Implementing bid placement as a plain read-then-write without a compare-and-set or lock, which works fine in testing and silently loses bids under real concurrent load.
- ⚠️ Treating auto-bid as 'just place the max bid immediately,' which reveals a bidder's true maximum to competitors instead of the minimum needed to stay ahead, defeating the entire point of proxy bidding.
- ⚠️ Using client-side polling for outbid notifications, which is both slow and puts unnecessary read load on the system exactly during high-contention auction endings.
- ⚠️ Closing an auction with a simple 'find all auctions where end_time has passed' cron job that isn't idempotent, risking a race with a very late-arriving bid or a duplicate close event.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why is 'read the current highest bid, then write the new one' unsafe, and what specifically fixes it?**

**Q: How would auto-bid cascades interact with anti-sniping extension logic?**

> **Model Answer:** A cascade of auto-bid counter-bids happening in the final seconds should trigger the same end-time extension as a manual bid would, since from the auction's perspective new bidding activity occurred right before close, regardless of whether a human or the auto-bid system generated it. This needs to be handled inside the same atomic bid-accepting operation so the extension logic sees the final state of the cascade, not an intermediate one.

**Q: Why might a per-auction dedicated sequencer scale better than relying purely on database row locks for very hot auctions?**

> **Model Answer:** Database row locks under extreme contention cause many transactions to block and retry, adding latency and burning database connections exactly when load is highest. A dedicated in-memory sequencer (one lightweight process or actor per active hot auction) processes that auction's bids strictly in order with no lock contention at all, at the cost of needing failover logic so that if the sequencer instance dies, another can take over without losing in-flight state.

# Design an Auction System (eBay)

> **Difficulty:** `MEDIUM` | **Target Companies:** `eBay` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> A bid is not just a write, it's a comparison-and-write against a value that a hundred other people might be racing to change at the exact same instant, so the entire design is about making 'is this the new highest bid' atomic under real concurrency, not about storing bids.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design an online auction system like eBay: a seller lists an item with a
starting price and an end time, buyers place bids, the highest bid at the
close of the auction wins. Support both manual bids and "auto-bid" (a
buyer sets a max they're willing to pay and the system bids incrementally
on their behalf up to that max). Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: How does auto-bidding (proxy bidding) actually work, does the system bid the minimum increment needed to stay ahead, up to the user's max?
*Why it matters:* This changes bid placement from a simple insert into a small state machine: every new manual bid can trigger an automatic counter-bid from an existing auto-bidder, which itself might trigger another, so the design needs to handle a bidding cascade within a single request, not just one write.

#### Q: What happens if two bids arrive at nearly the same instant, does strict ordering matter, and how do we prevent both from being accepted as 'the new highest'?
*Why it matters:* This is the core concurrency problem of the whole system. Without an atomic compare-and-set on the current highest bid, two concurrent requests can both read the same 'old highest' and both think they won, corrupting the auction state.

#### Q: Does the auction end time extend if a bid comes in during the last moments (anti-sniping), or is it a hard cutoff?
*Why it matters:* A hard cutoff makes 'close the auction' a simple scheduled job. Anti-sniping extension means closing an auction is itself a dynamic, bid-dependent decision, and the scheduling system has to be able to push its own deadline back in response to new writes.

#### Q: How many concurrent bidders does a single hot auction realistically see, is this closer to a handful of bidders or thousands racing on a single popular item?
*Why it matters:* A handful of bidders can be safely serialized with an ordinary database transaction. Thousands of concurrent bidders on one item turn that same row into a hot lock contention point, which changes the concurrency strategy from 'a transaction' to something that needs a queue or a dedicated serialization point per auction.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A seller can create an auction listing with a starting price, item details, and an end time.
- A buyer can place a manual bid on an active auction, which must exceed the current highest bid by at least the minimum increment.
- A buyer can set a maximum auto-bid amount, and the system automatically places incremental bids on their behalf to keep them winning, up to that maximum.
- The system determines and announces the winning bidder when an auction closes, and notifies outbid users promptly during the auction.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Bid placement must be strongly consistent: under concurrent bids for the same auction, exactly one bid is ever recorded as the current highest, no lost updates.**
- **Outbid notifications should reach affected users within a couple of seconds, close to real-time, since a delayed notification directly costs a bidder the auction.**
- **The system must remain available and responsive during the closing seconds of popular auctions, which is exactly when bid volume spikes hardest.**
- **Auction close timing must be reliable and precise, an auction that closes late or early is a direct, disputable integrity failure of the product.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 5 million active auctions at any time, average auction runs for 5 days
- Average auction receives 15 bids over its lifetime, but the top 1% of 'hot' auctions receive over 500 bids, concentrated heavily in the final minute
- 50 million bids placed per day platform-wide
- A hot auction in its final minute can see up to 20 bids/sec from a bidding war combined with auto-bid cascades

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Average bid write rate:** 50,000,000 / 86,400 seconds ≈ 580 bids/sec average across the whole platform, spread over millions of auctions so contention per auction is normally low
- **Peak contention on one hot auction:** 20 bids/sec sustained for the last 60 seconds of a hot auction means up to 1,200 competing writes against the same 'current highest bid' value in a single minute
- **Auto-bid cascade multiplier:** If 3 auto-bidders are active on one item, a single manual bid can trigger up to 2 additional automatic counter-bids in the same instant, roughly tripling the effective write rate on that one auction's hot path during a bidding war
- **Notification fan-out:** Each of the ~1,200 bids on a hot auction in its final minute potentially outbids the previous highest bidder, meaning up to 1,200 outbid notifications need to go out for that single item in that single minute

*Capacity Takeaway:* The platform-wide bid rate is modest, under 600 bids/sec on average, but the real problem is concentrated: a single hot auction's last 60 seconds can generate more write contention on one row than the rest of the platform generates in total, which is why per-auction bid serialization, not overall throughput, is the number that drives this architecture.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
A bid submitted to POST /bids does not go straight to a naive insert.
Instead, each auction has a single logical serialization point (either a
database row with optimistic concurrency control via the version field, or
a per-auction in-memory actor/queue for very hot auctions) that every bid
for that auction must pass through one at a time. The app server reads the
current highest bid and version, validates the new bid against it, and
attempts an atomic compare-and-set write; if it fails because another bid
won the race, it retries against the new current state. After a bid is
accepted, the system checks active auto-bid settings for that auction and
synchronously generates any necessary counter-bids through the same
serialization point, then publishes an outbid event asynchronously so the
previous highest bidder is notified without blocking the bid response
itself.

#### Bid placement through a per-auction serialization point

```mermaid
flowchart LR

    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client"]:::client
    lb["Load Balancer"]:::server
    app["App Servers"]:::server
    seq["Auction Bid Sequencer"]:::server
    auctiondb[("Auctions DB")]:::db
    bidsdb[("Bids History")]:::db
    queue>"Outbid Events Queue"]:::queue
    notify["Notification Workers"]:::server
    client --> lb
    lb --> app
    app -->|"submit bid"| seq
    seq -->|"CAS on current highest"| auctiondb
    seq -->|"append bid"| bidsdb
    seq -.->|"outbid event"| queue
    queue -.-> notify
```

#### A bid that triggers an auto-bid counter-bid

#### Choosing how to serialize bids on one auction

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  a["Expected concurrent bidders?"] --> b["Handful"]
  a --> c["Hundreds, hot auction"]
  b --> d["Ordinary DB transaction"]
  c --> e["Version-based compare-and-set"]
  e --> f["Conflicts under extreme load?"]
  f -->|"Yes"| g["Per-auction sequencer actor"]
  f -->|"No"| e
```

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/api/auctions` | Body: { item_details, starting_price, end_time }. Creates a new auction listing from the authenticated seller. |
| `POST` | `/api/auctions/{auctionId}/bids` | Body: { amount } for a manual bid, or { max_auto_bid } to set/update proxy bidding. Atomically validates against the current highest bid and either accepts or rejects with the current price. |
| `GET` | `/api/auctions/{auctionId}` | Returns the auction's current state: current highest bid (amount only, not the bidder's max), time remaining, and bid history. |
| `POST` | `/api/auctions/{auctionId}/watch` | Subscribes the authenticated user to real-time updates (outbid notifications, closing alerts) for this auction. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `auctions`
- `auction_id (unique)`
- `seller_id`
- `starting_price`
- `current_highest_bid_amount`
- `current_highest_bidder_id`
- `end_time (mutable if anti-sniping extension applies)`
- `status (active, closed, cancelled)`
- `version (optimistic concurrency token, incremented on every bid)`
*Notes:* The version field is what makes bid placement safe: a bid write includes a compare-and-set against the version it read, so two concurrent bids can never both succeed against the same stale state.

### Entity: `bids`
- `bid_id`
- `auction_id (indexed)`
- `bidder_id`
- `amount`
- `is_auto_bid (bool)`
- `placed_at (timestamp)`
*Notes:* An append-only history, never updated, so the full bid trail is always auditable, which matters a lot for dispute resolution.

### Entity: `auto_bid_settings`
- `auction_id`
- `bidder_id`
- `max_amount`
- `active (bool)`
*Notes:* Stores the private max a user is willing to pay. Never exposed to other bidders or the seller, only used internally to generate counter-bids.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### Making 'place a bid' atomic under real concurrency
The naive approach, read the current highest bid, check the new bid beats it, then write, has a race condition: two concurrent requests can both read the same old highest bid, both pass validation, and both write, with the second write silently overwriting the first's win instead of being rejected. # Design a Food Delivery App (DoorDash)

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `DoorDash • Uber Eats` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> This is a **three-sided marketplace**, not a two-sided one, and the genuinely hard problem is that a single order is a live ==state machine== three different parties are simultaneously watching and acting on, so the design has to answer 'who is allowed to move this order forward, and how does everyone else find out' before it answers anything about menus or maps.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a food delivery app like DoorDash: customers browse nearby
restaurants and place orders, restaurants accept and prepare those orders,
and drivers pick up food and deliver it. All three sides need to see the
order's status update in near real time as it moves through the process.
Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: How many active drivers and restaurants are we assuming per city, and how tight does driver-order matching need to be geographically?
*Why it matters:* If matching only needs to consider drivers within a couple of kilometers, a geospatial index keyed by city or grid cell works. If matching has to reason about traffic, driver direction, and multiple in-flight orders per driver, the matching service becomes a much bigger optimization problem, closer to ride-hailing dispatch.

#### Q: Does the customer need live GPS tracking of the driver on a map, or is a coarse status ('out for delivery') enough?
*Why it matters:* Live GPS tracking means drivers push location updates every few seconds and those updates fan out to an open customer connection, which is a sustained real-time streaming workload. A coarse status is just an occasional state transition, a much cheaper problem.

#### Q: Can a restaurant reject an order after the customer has already paid, and how long does a restaurant have to accept?
*Why it matters:* If restaurants can reject or time out, the order state machine needs a defined 'awaiting restaurant confirmation' state with a deadline, plus a refund path, rather than assuming every paid order is automatically accepted.

#### Q: Is a driver allowed to carry multiple orders at once (batched delivery), or exactly one order per driver at a time?
*Why it matters:* Single-order-per-driver keeps matching a straightforward nearest-available-driver lookup. Batching means the matching and routing logic has to reason about pickup sequencing and combined ETAs across restaurants, which is a materially harder assignment problem.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A customer can browse restaurants near their location and place an order with one or more items.
- A restaurant can see incoming orders, accept or reject them, and mark an order as being prepared and then ready for pickup.
- The system assigns the order to a nearby available driver, who picks it up from the restaurant and delivers it to the customer.
- All three parties (customer, restaurant, driver) see the order's current status update in near real time as it moves through the process.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Order state transitions must be reliable and visible to all three parties within a few seconds, stale or missing status updates directly damage trust in the product.**
- **Driver matching must be fast, a customer should not wait more than a few seconds to learn whether a driver has been found.**
- **The system must handle regional spikes gracefully (a Friday night rush in one city should not degrade order placement in another city).**
- **The order record itself must be durable and consistent: once a customer sees 'order placed,' the order cannot silently be lost even if a downstream service (matching, notifications) fails.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 10 million daily active customers across all cities, 500,000 active drivers, 300,000 active restaurants
- Average customer places an order every 3 days that they order at all, with 30% of DAUs ordering on a given day
- Average order takes 35 minutes end to end (accept, prepare, pickup, deliver), generating roughly 6 status updates over its lifetime
- Each active driver, while on a delivery, pushes a location ping every 5 seconds

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Orders placed per day:** 10,000,000 * 30% = 3 million orders/day ≈ 35 orders/sec average, several times that at dinner-hour peaks
- **Status update fan-out events per day:** 3,000,000 orders * 6 status changes * 3 parties notified = 54 million notification events/day ≈ 625/sec average
- **Driver location pings at peak:** Assume 150,000 drivers actively on a delivery at dinner peak * 1 ping per 5 sec = 30,000 pings/sec, which is the single largest stream of writes in the whole system
- **Matching lookups per day:** 3,000,000 orders * 1 matching request (plus retries for ~10% that need re-matching) ≈ 3.3 million geospatial queries/day ≈ 38/sec average, cheap compared to location pings

*Capacity Takeaway:* Order volume itself is modest (tens of orders/sec), but continuous driver location pings dominate write volume by three orders of magnitude, which means the driver-location path needs its own lightweight, high-throughput store, it cannot share infrastructure with the durable order/database path.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
Three services sit behind an API gateway. An Order Service owns the order
state machine end to end and is the only writer to the orders table; every
transition (accept, prepare, ready, pick up, deliver) is validated against
the current state before being applied. A Matching Service takes a newly
placed order, queries a geospatial index (drivers' live locations, kept in
a fast in-memory store, not the relational database) for nearby available
drivers, and assigns one using proximity and estimated food-ready time. A
Notification Service subscribes to order status events off a queue and
pushes updates to the customer, restaurant, and driver over persistent
connections (WebSocket or long-lived push), so no party has to poll. Driver
location pings flow into the geospatial store directly, bypassing the
order database entirely, since they're high-frequency and ephemeral, only
the order's pickup/delivery timestamps need to be durable.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Order placement, matching, and live tracking

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Customer/Restaurant/Driver Apps"]:::client
    gateway["API Gateway"]:::server
    orderservice["Order Service"]:::server
    orderdb[("Orders DB")]:::db
    matching["Matching Service"]:::server
    geo["Geospatial Store"]:::cache
    queue>"Status Events Queue"]:::queue
    notify["Notification Service"]:::server
    client --> gateway
    gateway -->|"place/update order"| orderservice
    orderservice -->|"write state"| orderdb
    orderservice -->|"find driver"| matching
    matching -->|"nearby query"| geo
    client -.->|"location pings"| geo
    orderservice -.->|"status changed"| queue
    queue -.-> notify
    notify -.->|"push update"| client
```

#### Life of an order: placed to delivered

#### Order state machine, including reject and re-match paths

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  placed["placed"] --> confirm{"Restaurant accepts?"}
  confirm -->|"yes"| preparing["preparing"]
  confirm -->|"no / timeout"| refund["cancelled, refunded"]
  preparing --> ready["ready_for_pickup"]
  ready --> matched{"Driver confirms pickup?"}
  matched -->|"yes"| pickedup["picked_up"]
  matched -->|"no / timeout"| rematch["re-match new driver"]
  rematch --> matched
  pickedup --> delivered["delivered"]
```

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `GET` | `/api/restaurants/nearby` | Query params: lat, lng, radius. Returns restaurants near the customer, backed by a geospatial index, not the transactional restaurant table. |
| `POST` | `/api/orders` | Body: { restaurantId, items, deliveryAddress }. Creates an order in 'awaiting restaurant confirmation' state and charges payment. |
| `PATCH` | `/api/orders/{orderId}/status` | Body: { status }. Restaurant or driver transitions the order to its next valid state (accepted, preparing, ready, picked_up, delivered). |
| `POST` | `/api/drivers/{driverId}/location` | Body: { lat, lng, timestamp }. High-frequency location ping from the driver's app while on an active delivery. |
| `GET` | `/api/orders/{orderId}/track` | Server-sent stream or long-poll endpoint returning live order status and, if applicable, driver location, for the customer's tracking screen. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `orders`
- `order_id (unique)`
- `customer_id, restaurant_id, driver_id (nullable until matched)`
- `status (placed, accepted, preparing, ready_for_pickup, picked_up, delivered, cancelled)`
- `items, total_price, created_at, updated_at`
*Notes:* The single source of truth for the order state machine. Every status transition is written here first, then fanned out as an event, never the other way around.

### Entity: `order_status_events`
- `event_id`
- `order_id (indexed)`
- `status, actor (customer, restaurant, driver, system), timestamp`
*Notes:* Append-only audit log of every transition. Lets support/disputes reconstruct exactly what happened and when, separate from the mutable current-state orders row.

### Entity: `drivers`
- `driver_id (unique)`
- `current_status (offline, available, en_route)`
- `current_location (lat, lng, kept fresh via the geospatial index, not this row directly)`
- `active_order_id (nullable)`
*Notes:* current_location is logically here but physically lives in the fast geospatial store (see bottlenecks), this row is the durable driver record.

### Entity: `restaurants`
- `restaurant_id (unique)`
- `location (lat, lng)`
- `menu_id, is_accepting_orders (boolean)`
- `avg_prep_time_minutes`
*Notes:* avg_prep_time_minutes feeds the driver-matching service so it can time driver arrival to roughly coincide with food being ready, not before.

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `DoorDash • Uber Eats` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> This is a **three-sided marketplace**, not a two-sided one, and the genuinely hard problem is that a single order is a live ==state machine== three different parties are simultaneously watching and acting on, so the design has to answer 'who is allowed to move this order forward, and how does everyone else find out' before it answers anything about menus or maps.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a food delivery app like DoorDash: customers browse nearby

and drivers pick up food and deliver it. All three sides need to see the
order's status update in near real time as it moves through the process.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: How many active drivers and restaurants are we assuming per city, and how tight does driver-order matching need to be geographically?
*Why it matters:* If matching only needs to consider drivers within a couple of kilometers, a geospatial index keyed by city or grid cell works. If matching has to reason about traffic, driver direction, and multiple in-flight orders per driver, the matching service becomes a much bigger optimization problem, closer to ride-hailing dispatch.

#### Q: Does the customer need live GPS tracking of the driver on a map, or is a coarse status ('out for delivery') enough?
*Why it matters:* Live GPS tracking means drivers push location updates every few seconds and those updates fan out to an open customer connection, which is a sustained real-time streaming workload. A coarse status is just an occasional state transition, a much cheaper problem.

#### Q: Can a restaurant reject an order after the customer has already paid, and how long does a restaurant have to accept?
*Why it matters:* If restaurants can reject or time out, the order state machine needs a defined 'awaiting restaurant confirmation' state with a deadline, plus a refund path, rather than assuming every paid order is automatically accepted.

#### Q: Is a driver allowed to carry multiple orders at once (batched delivery), or exactly one order per driver at a time?
*Why it matters:* Single-order-per-driver keeps matching a straightforward nearest-available-driver lookup. Batching means the matching and routing logic has to reason about pickup sequencing and combined ETAs across restaurants, which is a materially harder assignment problem.

- A customer can browse restaurants near their location and place an order with one or more items.

# Design a Coupon/Discount System

> **Difficulty:** `EASY` | **Target Companies:** `Amazon • Shopify` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> A coupon code is really a **shared counter** with a hard ceiling, and the entire design problem is making sure thousands of customers racing to redeem the same popular code at the same moment can never push that counter past its cap, which is a ==concurrency problem== wearing a discounts costume.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a coupon and discount system for an e-commerce checkout: a customer
enters a coupon code at checkout, the system validates it (is it real, is
it expired, has this customer already used it, has it hit its global
redemption cap) and applies the discount. Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Does a coupon have both a global usage cap (e.g. 'first 10,000 redemptions') and a per-user cap (e.g. 'once per customer'), or only one of those?
*Why it matters:* A per-user-only cap is a simple keyed lookup against that one customer's redemption history. A global cap under high concurrency is the harder problem, since it requires coordinating a single shared counter across every concurrent checkout in the system, which changes the storage and locking strategy entirely.

#### Q: Can multiple coupons be stacked on a single order, or is it strictly one coupon per checkout?
*Why it matters:* Stacking means validation has to check compatibility rules between coupons (some combos allowed, some explicitly excluded), not just validate one code in isolation, which adds a rules-evaluation layer on top of simple cap checking.

#### Q: Is a coupon's validity based purely on its expiry date, or can it also be restricted by product category, minimum cart value, or specific SKUs?
*Why it matters:* Pure expiry-date validation is a cheap timestamp comparison. Category or SKU-scoped restrictions mean the validation step has to inspect actual cart contents against the coupon's rule set, which is a materially heavier check that has to happen on every checkout attempt, not just once.

#### Q: If a coupon redemption succeeds but the overall order later fails or is cancelled, should the coupon usage be automatically released back?
*Why it matters:* If yes, redemption isn't final until order confirmation, which means the system needs a reservation-then-confirm flow (similar to inventory) rather than a single atomic decrement, directly shaping whether redemption count is decremented eagerly or held provisionally.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A customer can enter a coupon code at checkout, and the system validates whether it's currently valid (exists, not expired, not yet at its usage cap).
- The system enforces a global redemption cap on a coupon (e.g. 'only the first 10,000 uses succeed') without ever allowing more redemptions than the cap.
- The system enforces a per-user redemption cap (e.g. 'each customer may use this code at most once').
- A valid coupon's discount is correctly applied to the order total before payment is charged.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Coupon validation must be fast, well under a couple hundred milliseconds, since it sits directly in the checkout critical path.**
- **The global redemption cap must never be exceeded, even when thousands of customers attempt to redeem the same popular code in the same second (e.g. a flash-sale code posted publicly).**
- **The system must remain correct under concurrent access without serializing all checkouts through a single lock that would make checkout itself slow for everyone.**
- **Coupon rule changes (a code being disabled or its cap being reduced) should take effect quickly, within a few seconds, not require a full system redeploy.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 5 million checkouts per day, of which 15% attempt to apply a coupon code
- A viral, publicly shared code can see a redemption burst of up to 5,000 attempts within a single second when a limited-time deal is announced
- 1 million active coupon codes at any given time, most with modest caps (hundreds to low thousands), a small number with caps in the tens of thousands
- Each validation check involves a cap lookup, a per-user history lookup, and a rule-compatibility check

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Coupon validation attempts per day:** 5,000,000 * 15% = 750,000 attempts/day ≈ 8.7/sec average, trivial in isolation
- **Peak burst on one viral code:** 5,000 concurrent redemption attempts within one second against a single coupon's counter, this is the number that breaks a naive read-then-write validation
- **Successful redemptions vs failed attempts on a capped code:** If a code caps at 10,000 and gets a 5,000/sec burst, the system must correctly let exactly 10,000 through and reject the rest within milliseconds each, not queue them
- **Per-user redemption history size:** 1,000,000 active codes * average 3% of active customers redeem each ≈ tens of millions of (user, coupon) rows, easily indexed by a composite key

*Capacity Takeaway:* Average throughput here is trivially low, the entire design problem is concentrated in a few seconds of extreme contention on a single popular code's counter, which is exactly the kind of hot-key concurrency problem that decides whether the cap is actually enforced or silently oversold.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
A Coupon Service sits in the checkout path behind the same API gateway as
cart and order services. Validation first does the cheap checks (does the
code exist, is it expired, does the cart satisfy its rules) against a
cached copy of the coupon's rule metadata, since that data changes rarely.
Only if those pass does it attempt the actual redemption: an atomic
conditional decrement against the coupon's redemption counter (kept in a
fast in-memory store, not a row-locked relational table), which either
succeeds (a slot was available) or fails fast (cap already hit). A
successful redemption is recorded as 'reserved' tied to the in-progress
order, and only flips to 'confirmed' once the order itself confirms; if
the order fails, the reservation is released and the counter is
incremented back. This mirrors the inventory reserve-then-confirm pattern,
because a coupon cap is structurally the same problem as a stock count.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Coupon validation and atomic redemption

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Checkout Client"]:::client
    gateway["API Gateway"]:::server
    coupon["Coupon Service"]:::server
    rulecache["Rule Cache"]:::cache
    counter["Redemption Counter Store"]:::cache
    db[("Coupons/Redemptions DB")]:::db
